item.title: French Polynesia Cabin Cruise: The Floating Boutique Hotel for Effortless Island Hopping
item.description: Imagine waking up in a comfortable suite aboard a premium catamaran. You stretch out on crisp sheets and wonder what spectacular view is awaiting you today. Will it be the majestic twin peaks of Bora Bora or the white sand beaches and tropical jungles of Huahine? You step on deck and sniff the air: today’s port is actually the vanilla-scented shores of Taha’a. That’s what life is like aboard a French Polynesia cabin cruise. Every day, you get to go on a new adventure. At night, you rest and relax in the comfort of a spacious cabin aboard a shared catamaran charter. For many travelers, the freedom to visit multiple destinations rather than be confined to a single resort makes a cabin cruise a much better option than a typical holiday on land. What Is a French Polynesia Cabin Cruise? A French Polynesia catamaran cruise or cabin cruise is a travel option where you book a private cabin with its own attached bathroom on a catamaran. Instead of chartering an entire yacht yourself, you share the vessel with a small group of other travelers. How Cabin Cruises Work The catamaran operates much like a small-scale cruise ship but with a personalized touch. Your captain navigates the islands, and an onboard steward prepares your meals. This vacation style eliminates the stress of trip planning, sailing logistics, and meal preparation. And since vessels are shared among travelers, cabin cruises are more affordable than booking Tahiti yacht charters . Why It Feels Like a Floating Boutique Hotel Unlike massive cruise ships that carry thousands of passengers, a catamaran hosts between 8 and 12 guests. This creates an intimate atmosphere, similar to that of a small hotel, except you also get to experience different destinations and activities every day. In French Polynesia, our cabin cruises are offered on the Bali 5.4, Lagoon 620, and the Fountaine Pajot Ipanema 58, each accommodating 12 guests. Comfort and Convenience: What Is a Cabin Cruise Like Onboard? Life aboard a cabin charter is defined by relaxation and comfort. Your catamaran features decks, shaded outdoor dining areas, and a forward trampoline net. This net is a great spot to lounge as the islands glide by. No jostling for sunbathing space on crowded beaches or lining up to rent gear from stands along the shore. You can get all the sun you want on deck, and the cruise includes the use of water sports equipment. You can step directly off the yacht’s transom steps into the water, swim, snorkel, or kayak to your heart’s content. Island Hopping Without Repacking or Airport Transfers With 118 islands and atolls spread across an area as vast as Western Europe, French Polynesia island hopping is all about discovering the unique character of each destination. However, having your base camp be a hotel or resort limits your options. It also means you have to go through a drawn-out process of getting there before you can visit each different island. Traditional travelers must pack their suitcases, check out of their resorts, take a taxi to the airport, wait in security lines, and fly to the next island, only to repeat the check-in process. Meanwhile, on Tahiti cabin cruises , you unpack your bags once on arrival. While you relax on deck or sleep in your cabin, the catamaran moves you between Tahiti and other destinations like Huahine, Raiatea, Taha’a, and Bora Bora. A Tahiti cabin charter eliminates the need for regional flights and ferry schedules, saving you both travel stress and vacation time. Space, Food, Privacy, and Seasickness: Honest Answers Before booking a sailing trip, it is normal to have a few questions about how things work on a boat. Here is what daily life aboard your shared luxury catamaran looks like. Space: Yacht cabins are smaller than hotel rooms, but they’re just as well-appointed. They feature built-in storage and ensuite bathrooms, with air-conditioning at specified daylight hours when you want a break from the tropical heat. Food: Your steward handles all the grocery …

item.title: Why The Bali 5.4 Should be Your Next Charter
item.description: The Bali 5.4 brings together space, comfort, and performance all in an impeccably designed 54-foot catamaran perfect for charter vacations. This yacht was built with a focus on open bright living spaces, comfortable accommodations, and plentiful outdoor spaces. With room for up to 12 in its six-cabin configuration, the Bali 5.4 is perfect for social sailing. Dream Yacht guests have the option to enjoy this yacht through a cabin cruise or when the yacht has availability outside of cabin charters, book it as a crewed yacht charter for an exclusive experience with family and friends. A Layout Designed for Living The center of the Bali 5.4’s design was built around bringing people together while still allowing space to spread out. Fluid flowing spaces from bow to stern creates seamless connection between the outdoor living areas, saloon, and aft cockpit. One of the most distinctive and innovative features of this yacht is the large pivoting rear door. It excellently connects the salon with the aft cockpit creating one extended living area and allowing for a larger conversation space. Another unique feature is the sliding windows that allow for more airflow and light giving an open air feel throughout. Forward of the saloon a door provides easy access to the foredeck. Here cushioned seats stretch out into the sun allowing guests to relax and enjoy the views while underway. While the aft cockpit provides a perfect gathering space for lunch or dinner at anchor with comfortable seating. The davits and swim ladder on the stern provide an easy access to the water for swimming. Then above there is a flybridge with a large U shaped seating area perfect for sipping a morning coffee with the sunrise or sundowners after a rewarding day of cruising. Forward of the seating area find the sunbathing pads where guests can lounge while taking in the breathtaking scenery of one of Dream Yacht’s incredible destinations. This Bali 5.4 provides so many areas where connection to the natural world and each other become possible. Find peace and shared experiences through innovation and exploration aboard this yacht. Take the Tour Comfortable Accommodations Below Deck The Bali 5.4 continues to deliver through its focus on comfort as we move below deck. Each cabin is equipped with queen sized beds, a private bathroom with a shower, and adequate storage space. Natural light and airflow are still features even down in the cabins; some cabins even have direct access to the deck. For large groups this layout is meant to give everyone their own private space at night, while relishing the communal spaces during the day. Guests get the feeling of home and settling in through these comfortable areas instead of the fleeting feeling of a hotel room. Why Charter the Bali 5.4 Space for Everyone – Roughly 130 square meters of living space allows for plenty of room to dine, relax, and enjoy cruising without feeling crowded. Indoor/Outdoor Living – The yacht’s flow from bow to stern and one of a kind opening door from the saloon to the aft cabin makes it easy to roam between the interior and exterior living spaces. Enjoy the breeze blowing through the yacht which creates a light airy open feel that connects you to the natural beauty of the surrounding world. Relaxation Area Options – There is no shortage of lounging areas onboard from the flybridge to the foredeck choose your ideal spot to enjoy the sail from. Now Newly Available for Private Crewed Charters When a Bali 5.4 is not being used on a cabin charter it will be available for a private crewed charter experience with a captain and hostess. This means families or groups of friends can experience the entire yacht privately, with a professional crew taking care of the sailing, itinerary, food, and day to day operation. Allowing guests to concentrate on relaxation and taking in the scenery from any of the comfortable lounging areas. item.title: New BALI Catamarans arriving in the Seychelles
item.description: As Dream Yacht’s first base location and founding sailing destination nearly 25 years ago, the Seychelles Islands hold a place of honor in the hearts and minds of our Dream Yacht Worldwide charter team. Now we’re pleased to announce the arrival of two brand new catamarans soon to be available for charter in this very special island paradise. The new yachts, BALI 4.4 and BALI 4.6 catamarans, are now in transit arriving in December and available for charters from December 14, 2024. BALI yachts are one of our most sought-after charter brands, making these new 2024 “Super Premier” catamarans an exciting addition to our Seychelles fleet. About the new BALI Catamarans The BALI 4.4 is a 44-foot 4-cabin/4-bath catamaran, perfect for families or groups of friends up to 10 people. The 5-cabin/4-bath BALI 4.6 is 46-feet, and is well-suited for larger groups or for allowing space for a hired skipper. Both yachts feature the popular “garage-door” style pivoting door that creates an open air salon that lends itself to comfortable indoor/outdoor living. Both yachts also feature spacious flybridge lounge areas for comfortable seating with a view while underway, or for sunset gatherings. Sailing the Seychelles Islands We began our first Dream Yacht charters in the Seychelles for good reason. This Indian Ocean Island chain is arguably one of the most beautiful sailing grounds on the planet, with 41 of the earth’s oldest granite islands and 74 low-lying islands surrounded by brilliant blue waters and pristine reefs. For nature lovers, the bird watching, hiking, and snorkeling are unmatched. And a visit to the protected island of Curieuse to observe the gentle giant Aldabra tortoises and unique coco de mer palms is a must. Underscoring Dream Yacht’s strong commitment to delivering top sailing opportunities in the beautiful Seychelles, we will welcome additional BALI yachts – 2 BALI 4.8 catamarans – in the Seychelles late in 2025. Plan now for your dream Seychelles sailing vacation to secure one of these stunning new sailing catamarans. Get in touch with a Dream Yacht charter planner today! Share: Link Copied to Clipboard

item.title: What I Learned From Our One-Year Sailing Sabbatical
item.description: Chris DiCroce is an Amazon bestselling author, sailor, online educator, and speaker. He’s been featured in Sail Magazine, The Waterway Guide, Spinsheet Magazine, and various other magazines and podcasts. He spent 6 years cruising various parts of the U.S. and the Western Caribbean with his wife and dog, and 2 years traveling through Guatemala and Mexico. To learn more about Chris and his travels, visit mondovacilando.com . Read about his experience living on a yacht below… Have you ever wondered what it would be like to take a one-year sailing sabbatical and sail away from it all? Do you find yourself watching countless YouTube videos featuring bronze bodies and beautiful sailboats anchored in the turquoise waters surrounding some faraway island? I know exactly how you feel. For years, I also dreamt of warm breezes and salty waves. After a stream of layoffs at my job left me searching for answers, I decided to go for it. The only thing that needed to happen in order for this dream to become reality was to convince my wife Melody to get onboard – literally. After many late-night discussions, we came to the conclusion that life is short. Time is precious. We said, “What good is having a dream if you never go for it?” So, on a glorious weekend, I, Melody, and our dog Jet loaded up our 35-foot sailboat and hit the high seas for what was to be our one-year escape. Casting Off the Dock Lines We sailed south along the east coast of the United States, bound for Cuba and the Western Caribbean. Once the butter started to melt, we knew we were closer to our ideal latitude. We adjusted quickly to our new life. The concerns we had about the lack of space or how Jet would adapt to life on a sailboat faded. As a matter of fact, when we saw the sun rise over the city of Havana, any remaining doubts about whether our sailing sabbatical was the right decision drifted off with the seafoam. It was a morning we’ll never forget. Cuban immigration officials were both shocked and amused that we were sailing with a 50 lb. dog. They had a lot of questions about how and where he goes to the bathroom. Of course we all had a good laugh as Melody and I tried to explain, in our mediocre Spanish, that getting Jet to go on deck was proving to be a test of wills. But once the officials were satisfied we had all the correct paperwork and international health certificates, Jet got his stamp of approval. We spent fourteen days exploring Havana’s bustling streets. We discovered quaint local eateries, amazing art galleries, and off-the-beaten-track neighborhoods. When we left, we sailed west along the north coast in some of the bluest water I’ve ever seen. We anchored in deserted bays and sipped our Havana Club rum as we watched the sun tuck itself in for the night. We crossed the Yucatan Channel and spent three incredible weeks anchored in the Makax Lagoon in Isla Mujeres. We learned a little more Spanish and immersed ourselves further into our cruiser personas. In our minds, a one-year sailing sabbatical wasn’t much time. We wanted to experience as much as possible, so we moved often. And we kept moving. We kept exploring. We sailed south to Belize, where we snorkeled the out islands and took in the spectacular reef that is second only to the Great Barrier Reef of Australia. Melody and I were in the water at dawn and in our bunk before 9. Sailing With a Dog Jet seemed to love his new aquatic life as well. I mean, who wouldn’t love long strolls on deserted beaches and endless belly rubs from strangers in the beach bar? But sailing with a dog presents some challenges. He’s a shepherd and he sheds a lot, therefore, we vacuum constantly. And yes, there’s the bathroom issue on longer passages. Jet refused to use the fake grass pad that we put on deck for his potty breaks. He gave in a few times when there was no alternative, but more often than not, we planned our route and our stops so that it afforded us the ability to land a dinghy and take him to shore.
